study.title: Psalm 140 - Deliverment of the righteous and judgment on the violent
study.overview: Psalm 140 is a supplication of David for protection from perverse and violent enemies, described as people who plan wickedness, use poisonous words and trap gun. The psalmist not only asks for ransom, but also presents his confidence that the Lord will hear his cause, will thwart the project of the wicked and will make the righteous end in gratitude and communion before God. The psalm combines mourning, request for help, desire for justice and certainty of vindication.

outline.title: Request for deliverance against corrupt enemies
outline.explanation: David begins supplicating that the LORD keep him from evil and violent men. These adversaries are portrayed as people who continually plan wickedness and hurt with words compared to the serpent venom. The image shows that the danger is not only physical, but also verbal and moral.

outline.title: Protection against traps and falls
outline.explanation: The psalmist again asks that God preserves him from the hands of the wicked and the plans of the arrogant. The metaphors of loops, nets and traps show calculated persecution, as if the life of the righteous was surrounded by hidden stratagems.

outline.title: Trust in God and asked to thwart evil
outline.explanation: David confesses the Lord as his God and asks him for attention. He calls the LORD the strength of his salvation and reminds that God has already protected him in battle. Then asks that the desires and plans of the wicked do not prosper, so that they do not magnify themselves because of evil.

outline.title: Judgment on the wicked and certainty of vindication
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks that the evil of the adversaries fall upon them and that the violent does not establish itself. He then affirms his conviction that the Lord will defend the cause of the afflicted and the right of the needy. The psalm ends with the hope of public gratitude of the righteous and their permanence before the presence of God.

study.context: The text is presented as a psalm of David, given to the regent. The notes provided relate him to the period in which David was persecuted, especially by Saul, and even suggest, in a commented tradition, a situation of concrete and violent threat. These references help to read the psalm as someone's prayer pressured by real enemies, but the chapter itself focuses more on moral and spiritual conflict than in historical details.
study.theology: The psalm states that God sees wickedness hidden, hears the supplication of the afflicted and is able to prevent the ungodly triumph. It also shows that words can be instruments of violence, so injustice is not limited to physical acts. At the same time, the text teaches that God's righteousness includes defense of the needy and judgment of the wicked. The conclusion is important: the hope of the righteous ends not only in survival, but in gratitude and in dwelling before the face of God, that is, in communion and divine favor. The language of judgment is strong and must be read as a cry for justice, not as human permission for personal revenge.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is an individual lament in which the psalmist asks the Lord for protection and ransom, confident in the strength and justice of God.
David is presented as one who suffers before he is exalted, so that his experience points out kindly to Christ, who was also humiliated before he was glorified.
The psalmist asks for the deliverance of the evil man, identified in the note as Saul, who persecuted David with envy, cruelty and violence.

questions: How does the description of enemies as poisonous-speaking people broaden our view of what is violence?
What changes in prayer when the psalmist calls the Lord his God and the strength of his salvation?
How does the confidence that God defends the cause of the afflicted corrects our tendency to seek immediate vengeance?
study.practice: In facing opposition, this psalm teaches us to take the case directly to the Lord, without denying the gravity of evil and without trying to solve everything with retaliation. The concrete application is to cultivate honest prayer, discern destructive words and projects around us, and rest in the fact that God knows the cause of the afflicted. Instead of feeding hatred, we are called to ask for protection, persevere in integrity, and expect the righteous judgment of God, trusting that He sustains the needy and leads the righteous to their presence.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided suggest a context of persecution by Saul, but this is presented as an interpretive hypothesis, not as an uncontroversial data of the chapter. It is also not possible to affirm with certainty, only from the text and the notes, which specific events are behind each image of fire, pit and judgment. The confessional readings about Christ and hell appear in the notes as interpretations, not as explanations explicitly developed by the psalm.
